headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection, data leakage, and write conflicts between two broad-privilege coding agents.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystem content, and both use MCP; Goose explicitly shares state via filesystem, while Roo Code uses VS Code workspace files. That creates a default pathway where one agent can ingest the other’s outputs as trusted content. The interaction is documented enough to avoid guessing, but not isolated enough to call it low.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace or cwd, one agent can influence the other through file contents.
IF either agent treats workspace text as instructions, prompt injection becomes feasible.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories.
Disable automatic ingestion of generated files as instructions.
Use a human review step before copying outputs between agents.
Add provenance labels to files each agent writes.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace isolation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Goose touches files in the user filesystem and handles model-provider keys; Roo Code touches VS Code workspace files and browser screenshots. Because both share state via filesystem, sensitive code or screenshots can flow from one agent’s workspace into the other’s context in default use. The profiles do not show a hard isolation boundary, so medium is the safest choice.
conditions: IF the same repository or workspace is opened in both agents, files can be exposed across sessions.
IF either agent uploads file contents to its backend, shared workspace data can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace.
Use separate repos or clones per agent.
Redact screenshots and credentials before opening them in Roo Code.
Restrict file permissions on sensitive directories.
requires-engineering: add per-agent data-loss prevention controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, package installation, and git-state modification, and both share state via filesystem. In a shared repo, concurrent edits and git operations can overwrite each other or corrupt state without locking. This is a default-dangerous overlap with potentially irreversible work loss.
conditions: IF both agents modify the same git branch or working tree, conflicts and lost updates can occur.
IF either agent runs package installs or shell commands in the shared workspace, state can diverge unexpectedly.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Commit or stash changes before switching agents.
Use a lock file for shared mutable resources.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Both agents can act on files and shell commands, so one agent’s output can become the other’s input without a verification barrier. Roo Code’s browser and broader workspace access make it especially likely to operationalize Goose’s generated artifacts. The profiles do not prove blind trust, but the default workflow supports cascading mistakes.
conditions: IF Roo Code consumes Goose-generated files or terminal output as authoritative, errors can cascade.
IF Goose produces code or commands that Roo Code executes without review, downstream actions may be wrong.
mitigations: Require a verification step before execution.
Compare outputs against source files before acting.
Use small, isolated tasks instead of chained automation.
Review diffs before any git commit.
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and touch source code, but the provided data does not show a residency, certification, or retention mismatch. Goose handles model-provider keys and Roo Code handles browser screenshots, yet no regulated data class or jurisdictional constraint is documented here. The other agent is cited because the risk is pairwise, but the evidence only supports a low compliance concern.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is placed into the shared workspace, compliance review is required.
IF one agent is configured with a different retention policy than the other, records handling may diverge.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared workspaces.
Align retention settings before use.
Document which agent may process which data class.
Delete temporary screenshots after review.
requires-engineering: formalize residency and retention controls.
